rubric.why: Identifies budding as an outgrowth forming a bud in yeast.
rubric.description: A part of the parent yeast grows out and is called a bud.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the outgrowth and its name in yeast (or a unicellular fungus).

rubric.why: States what happens to the bud after it grows.
rubric.description: The grown bud may separate from the parent or remain attached.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both possible outcomes.

modelAnswer: This method is very common in yeast (a unicellular fungus). During budding, a part of the parent organism grows out from its body. This part is called a bud. When the bud has grown big, it may separate from parent body or may remain attached.

rubric.why: Identifies the nature of spores and the structure in which most fungi produce them.
rubric.description: Spores are thick-walled asexual reproductive cells produced in sac-like sporangia.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing spores as thick-walled asexual reproductive cells and identifying sporangia as their sacs.

rubric.why: Describes release of mature spores and their growth under favourable conditions.
rubric.description: The mature sporangium bursts, releasing spores that germinate in favourable conditions to form new fungus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for sporangium bursting and spores being released, then germinating in favourable conditions.

modelAnswer: Spores are thick-walled asexual reproductive cells. Most fungi (e.g. Rhizopus: bread mold) produce spores in special sac-like structures called sporangia (Singular: sporangium). When spores are mature, the sporangium bursts and spores are released. Spores can tolerate unfavourable conditions due to their thick walls. When favourable conditions are available, the spores germinate to produce new fungus.

rubric.why: Identifies the runner's structure and its position.
rubric.description: A runner (stolon) is a horizontal stem growing above the ground.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the runner is a horizontal stem above ground.

rubric.why: Explains how nodes form new plants.
rubric.description: Leaves and roots grow at nodes; a new plant forms there.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for connecting nodes, growth of leaves and roots, and formation of a new plant.

modelAnswer: Stolon (runner): It is a horizontal stem that grows above the ground. A stolon has nodes where new leaves and roots grow. The leaves grow upwards and roots grow down. In this way, a new plant is formed at the node. Strawberry reproduces by using its stolon.

rubric.why: Identifies the tuber as an underground fleshy stem.
rubric.description: A tuber is a fleshy stem that grows underground.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both the stem and underground location.

rubric.why: Explains that the tuber's eyes are buds that can produce plants.
rubric.description: The eyes are buds that can grow into new plants; potatoes reproduce by tubers.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying eyes as buds and stating that they grow into new plants.

modelAnswer: Tuber: It is fleshy stem that grows underground. It has “eyes” which are actually its buds. Eyes can grow into new plants. Potatoes reproduce by tubers.

rubric.why: States the advantage of rapid production of offspring with the parent's desirable characteristics.
rubric.description: Many plants can be produced quickly and are identical to the parent, retaining its useful qualities.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for rapid production and offspring being like the parent (with good characteristics passed on).

rubric.why: States the disadvantage of lack of variation and shared vulnerability.
rubric.description: Offspring have no genetic differences and are similarly vulnerable to environmental changes, diseases or pests.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for lack of variation/identical offspring and their shared susceptibility.

modelAnswer: Vegetative propagation allows to produce many new plants in a short time. The new plants are exactly like the parent plant, so they all have the same good characteristics. This means useful qualities, like good fruit or strong growth, are passed on to the next generation. Plants produced through vegetative propagation do not have genetic differences. In other words, all the offspring are identical. Due to it, they are equally sensitive to environmental changes and prone to the same diseases or pests.

rubric.why: Names the two outer flower whorls and their components.
rubric.description: Calyx consists of sepals; corolla consists of petals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both whorls and their correct components.

rubric.why: Names both reproductive whorls and their components.
rubric.description: Androecium consists of stamens, each with anther and filament; gynoecium consists of carpels with ovary, style and stigma.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the male and female whorls and all listed component parts.

modelAnswer: Calyx: It is the outermost whorl. It is made of green leaf-like sepals. Corolla: It is the second whorl and made of petals. Androecium: It is the third whorl and is made of male reproductive structures called stamens. Each stamen consists of an anther and a filament. Gynoecium: It is the innermost whorl made of the female reproductive structures called carpels. A carpel consists of three parts: ovary, style and stigma.

rubric.why: Describes meiosis in the megaspore mother cell and the resulting megaspores.
rubric.description: The diploid megaspore mother cell undergoes meiosis to produce four haploid megaspores, of which one survives.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for meiosis producing four haploid megaspores from the diploid mother cell.

rubric.why: Describes mitosis in the surviving megaspore, fusion of the polar nuclei and formation of the egg cell.
rubric.description: Mitosis forms eight haploid nuclei; two central nuclei fuse, and one of the remaining six forms the egg cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the eight nuclei, fusion of the two central nuclei, and formation of the egg cell from a remaining nucleus.

modelAnswer: The ovule acts as megasporangium. It contains a diploid megaspore mother cell which undergoes meiosis and produces four haploid megaspores. Only one megaspore remains alive. Inside megaspore, eight haploid nuclei are formed by mitosis. Two nuclei migrate to the center and fuse to form a fusion nucleus. One nucleus out of the remaining six forms the female gamete i.e., egg cell.

rubric.why: Defines asexual reproduction and identifies its offspring as genetically identical to the parent.
rubric.description: Asexual reproduction does not involve fusion of gametes; offspring are genetically identical to the parent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for no gamete fusion and genetically identical offspring.

rubric.why: Defines sexual reproduction and identifies variation among its offspring.
rubric.description: Sexual reproduction involves fusion of male and female gametes; offspring show variation among themselves and from parents.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for fusion of male and female gametes and variation in offspring.

modelAnswer: The reproduction that does not involve the fusion of gametes is called asexual reproduction. The offspring produced by asexual reproduction are genetically identical to the parents. On the other hand, the reproduction that involves the fusion of male and female gametes is called sexual reproduction. In sexual reproduction, the offspring have variations among themselves and with the parents.
